title: Acetate resonance
subtitle: The negative charge is shared by both oxygens

form-1.caption: sodium acetate, one resonance form
form-1.learnerPrompt: Draw the other resonance form of acetate. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
hintTiers: Which atom carries the negative charge, and is it next to a π bond?
The negative oxygen pushes a lone pair in to make a new C=O π bond. Carbon cannot have five bonds, so the old C=O π bond must move out at the same time. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of the negative oxygen into the C–O bond, making it double. Arrow 2: the C=O π bond onto the other oxygen, which becomes negative.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Resonance arrows never break or make σ bonds: the atoms stay exactly where they are. Move only lone pairs and π bonds.
The π pair moves towards oxygen, the more electronegative atom, not onto carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Carbon would now have five bonds, ten electrons. As the new π bond forms, the old C=O π bond must break: push it onto the other oxygen.

form-2.caption: sodium acetate, the other resonance form

steps.explanationAfterStep: The two forms are the same picture, mirrored. The real acetate ion is neither: each oxygen carries half a negative charge and each C–O bond is halfway between single and double. This sharing is why acetic acid is about a hundred billion times more acidic than ethanol.

mechanismSummary: A lone pair on the negative oxygen forms a C=O π bond, and the other C=O π bond moves onto its oxygen. The two forms are identical: the charge is shared equally, and both C–O bonds have the same length.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 7 (Delocalization and conjugation)
